data.title: Asia has less to fear from the AI correction than you might think
data.description:
IN THE semiconductor manufacturing hubs of Taiwan and South Korea, financial regulators are worried about the mounting risks of the artificial-intelligence boom.

On Nov 19, Taiwan’s Financial Supervisory Commission tightened curbs on short selling to help stabilise the stock market, after its benchmark index suffered its sharpest weekly decline since 1991.

Meanwhile, South Korean policymakers are considering activating a 10.7 trillion won (US$8 billion) stock market stabilisation fund. The Kospi has lost a staggering 48 per cent since hitting a record high on Jun 22.

It is hard to overstate the impact of the AI infrastructure build-out on Asia’s economies. In 2024, seven of the top 10 exporters of AI-enabling goods were in Asia, including Singapore and Malaysia, the only South-east Asian economies with front-end chip manufacturing capabilities.

The Asia-Pacific’s share of global data centre capacity is expected to exceed 40 per cent by 2030. Within the region, South-east Asia accounts for the largest proportion of capacity under construction, led by Malaysia and Thailand.

Gone are the days when the technology-heavy US stock market had the highest AI concentration risk.

In the MSCI Asia Pacific ex-Japan index, the information technology and communication services sectors have a combined 46 per cent weighting.

Taiwan and South Korea alone account for nearly 50 per cent of the entire emerging market equity index.

Asia under scrutiny

The dramatic unravelling of the AI trade across global markets since early October has put Asia under intense scrutiny. A succession of shocks has fanned fears over the financing, regulation and geopolitics of the AI build-out.

The plunge in US tech shares, the angst over the scale of AI-related debt issuance, and the threat of a clampdown on US data centre construction following the decisive victory of the Democrats in the midterm elections have undermined confidence in the AI narrative.

Moreover, the spying scandal engulfing Nvidia has ensnared South-east Asia, as US authorities scrutinise alleged chip diversion to China through the region.

New rules unveiled by the US Commerce Department seek to close a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s cutting-edge AI chips remotely by renting computing power from South-east Asian data centres and cloud providers.

The Institute for Progress, a US think tank, estimates remote access will account for nearly one-third of China’s AI chip stock by the end of next year, with South-east Asia expected to comprise 72 per cent of China’s overseas AI compute.

HSBC says “efforts to restrict mainland China’s access to advanced technology could become a broader investment and demand shock for (South-east Asia).”

Not so fast. While Asia is acutely vulnerable to a slowdown in the AI investment cycle, the region foreshadowed the financial and regulatory risks of the boom, helping blunt the impact of the recent turmoil in the US tech sector.

South Korea’s equity market was the canary in the coal mine for the AI trade. Foreign funds had already dumped US$130 billion of the country’s stocks in 2026 prior to the sell-off in the US, contributing to steep declines in Asian tech shares over the summer. This has made the region’s equity markets look increasingly undervalued, especially given the enduring strength of corporate earnings.

In a sign of the degree to which AI demand remains exceptionally buoyant, Goldman Sachs expects profit growth for the Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index in 2027 to reach 26 per cent, driven by the tech hardware and chip sectors in South Korea and Taiwan.

Regulatory realities

Furthermore, fears about the impact of tougher regulatory scrutiny of the AI build-out on South-east Asia’s economies are overdone.

While the new US-export licensing rules will test regional operators in the near term, the region has benefited from restrictions on data centre development designed to ensure the boom does not turn to bust.

Singapore’s full-blown moratorium on new construction in 2019 to 2022 was a catalyst for the surge in investment in the Malaysian state of Johor, currently the largest data centre market in the Asia-Pacific when combining operational and planned capacity.

It was also the precursor to the imposition of regulations across South-east Asia designed to balance sustainability requirements with digital infrastructure needs, creating a more resilient data centre market. The region’s neutrality, moreover, cuts both ways.

While many anchor tenants of data centres in Malaysia and Thailand are Chinese, a large portion is American. This “could divert more incremental demand towards (Malaysia) if (data centre) regulations tighten in the US”, notes Citigroup.

Lastly, it is important to put the threats to the AI build-out into perspective.

First, non-AI workloads – traditional compute and cloud services – accounted for nearly half of global data centre demand in 2025, said McKinsey.

In Asia, where digital infrastructure is at an earlier stage of the growth cycle, the share was much higher. Strong domestic and regional demand provide a buffer against a slowdown in the AI capital expenditure cycle.

Second, anti-data centre politicians’ bark is worse than their bite. In the US, Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic governor-elect of Texas – which accounts for one quarter of the nation’s planned data centre capacity – said construction of facilities with permits will be allowed to proceed.

In fact, stricter rules for approving new data centres should help ease concern over the financing of the AI boom. A slower, more expensive and selective build-out will increase the value of existing AI data centres, as the mismatch between strong demand and supply constraints intensifies.

Third, portfolio diversification in the age of AI is easier said than done, particularly in Asia.

While India is touted as the “anti-AI trade” because of its limited exposure to tech hardware, many fund managers see this as a liability and believe AI capital expenditure and monetisation will continue to drive returns in Asian equity markets.

The AI narrative remains compelling.

That Nvidia, under pressure from US President Donald Trump, reinstated the scandal-tainted Jensen Huang as its CEO shows that the build-out has a strong political backstop – one that limits how far lawmakers can let the AI trade unwind without hurting tens of trillions of dollars in American retirement savings.

Asia’s crucial role in the AI supply chain makes it a key gauge of investor sentiment. More volatility is inevitable. All the more reason not to lose sight of the powerful drivers of the region’s digital infrastructure boom.

The writer is an independent adviser and columnist

data.title: Stocks to watch: Kimly, AP Oil, Heptamax
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 26):

Kimly : The coffee shop operator reported a 30.8 per cent fall in net profit to S$12.8 million for its second half ended Sep 30, from S$18.5 million a year earlier. Revenue came in 1 per cent lower at S$161.1 million, from S$162.8 million previously. Kimly proposed a final dividend of S$0.01 a share for H2, bringing the total FY2026 dividend to S$0.02 a share. Shares of Kimly ended flat at S$0.365 on Wednesday, before the news.

AP Oil : The CEO of the petroleum products company, Ho Chee Hon, was sentenced to six months jail and a fine of S$25,000 for drink-driving on Wednesday. Accordingly, he will be away on a leave of absence for a period of six months from Dec 1. The company said that the charges are personal in nature and unrelated to its business or operations. Its board added that Ho remains suitable to continue in his role as CEO. Shares of AP Oil ended flat at S$0.126 on Wednesday, before the update.

Heptamax : The industrial solutions company, which is proposing to buy a data centre company for S$500 million in a reverse takeover, has been queried by the Singapore Exchange Regulation over the deal. Among other things, the regulator asked how the valuation for the target company Racks Central was arrived at. It also asked Heptamax to give details of the beneficial owners of the vendor. The company replied that the price was arrived at on a willing-buyer, willing-seller basis, taking into account Racks Central’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation for FY2025, among other things. Heptamax ended flat at S$0.131 on Wednesday.

data.title: Bankers pay up for Hong Kong apartments as rents hit new highs
data.description:
HONG Kong’s booming rental real estate market is spurring gains in previously underappreciated neighborhoods, as bankers pay up for apartments in one of the world’s most expensive places to live.

Ho Man Tin is luring finance professionals to the upscale neighborhood that’s near top schools and is close by to an area soon to house new office space for JPMorgan Chase & Co.

Rents in the area are up more than 15 per cent, almost double the pace of Hong Kong’s wider property market. Those in the increasingly popular Tseung Kwan O, far from the Central business district but connected by the underground rail network, are up 10 per cent. 

The old favourites are getting plenty of demand, too: Rents in Mid Levels, popular among European bankers attracted by its offering of restaurants and fancy delis, are up by double digits. Those in the Peak, home to many of the city’s richest people, have jumped more than 9 per cent.

Across the city, a sentiment shift that has fuelled a surge in initial public offerings and an office leasing rush among financial institutions is pushing rents ever higher.

Hong Kong’s rental price index of private homes jumped 6.3 per cent in the first ten months of this year, and average rental levels have repeatedly pushed to new record highs.

The frenzy is putting the pressure on potential renters, who are facing brief property listings and the risk of a form of a gazumping — a term from the market for home sales where buyers agree a deal and then find themselves pushed aside as a higher bid comes in at the last minute.

“The market hasn’t been this busy since at least 2018,” said Victoria Allan, founder and CEO of Habitat Property, which specialises in luxury properties. “We see shortages across all budget ranges, and some single-landlord buildings in Hong Kong Island south and Central have seen waiting lists.”

Gary Lee, an investment banker who leases a 600-square-feet apartment near his office in Central, said he didn’t hesitate when his landlord recently asked for a 10 per cent increase in rent.

“I don’t think I could find a similar available flat easily these days,” said the 35-year-old. Apartments “offering such convenience on transportation and shopping choices in nearby areas are limited.” 

No negotiations

Competition for rentals is being driven both by tight supply and a surge in demand. Expats are returning, white-collar workers and students are arriving from mainland China, and more confident local professionals are choosing to rent.

Hordes of foreigners are streaming back to grab white-collar jobs, responding to planned tax breaks for private equity and hedge funds. 

There’s also the impulse of government-led programmes designed to lure skilled professionals. More than 410,000 such approvals were granted over the last three years, with almost three-quarters arriving from mainland China, government data in March showed. 

Banking and fund management pros as well as high-net-worth individuals moving to the city through talent schemes are a major driver of rental growth, especially at the high-end, according to a residential leasing report by Savills.

With demand running ahead of available supply, landlords have gained greater pricing power and are increasingly preferring tenants from the financial services sector, the report shows.

The international property consultancy expects luxury residential rents will increase as much as 5 per cent in the final quarter of this year. 

It’s now a more ferocious environment where quick decisions can make or break a deal. 

“For years, a landlord’s asking price was always subject to negotiation, but now it’s a different story,” said property agent Sonam Thadani, who counts finance workers as one of her major client bases.

“We are coming to see tenants offering more than the asking price and willing to put down a deposit on the same day to secure a lease, especially where location and recent refurbishments offer limited competing options.”

Median asking prices for rents across Hong Kong rose about 7.9 per cent in the first ten months of 2026, with no neighborhood recording a decline over that period, according to property platform Spacious.hk.

The average time for each listing is also getting shorter, the data show. A typical two-bedroom flat around the prime Central area is fetching at least HK$25,000 (US$3,190) per month, not too far away from the average level in New York or Boston. 

Among popular areas, Ho Man Tin, an enclave in the centre of the Kowloon peninsula, emerged as the new winner on rental growth. It offers greater proximity to bankers working in West Kowloon and wealthy mainland Chinese families with children at international schools nearby, according to James Fisher, chief operating officer of Spacious.

JPMorgan is expected to move one of its offices into the West Kowloon area in 2028.  

Jennifer Zuo, a wealth management professional who moved to Hong Kong from Shanghai earlier this year, eventually settled on a fully furnished serviced apartment on the east side of Hong Kong island.

Zuo, who stumps up around HK$40,000 a month for the apartment, has already started thinking about her next move. Her rent will be up for negotiation next year — and she’s anticipating an increase. BLOOMBERG

data.description:

data.title: Stocks to watch: OCBC, Manulife US Reit
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Tuesday (Nov 24):

OCBC : The bank has appointed Ang Eng Siong, the current CEO of OCBC China, as its new head of global corporate banking from Jan 1, 2027. The appointment comes as the bank reorganises its wholesale banking business into three divisions. Under the new structure, Ang will lead what OCBC calls “GWB 1”, focusing on scaling the large corporate segment in its core markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Greater China – as well as its overseas branches. Shares of OCBC closed 0.5 per cent or S$0.13 lower at S$26.41 on Monday, before the announcement.

Manulife US Real estate investment trust (Reit) : The trust manager said that it has negotiated a proposed agreement with its lenders that would allow it to exit a three-year debt restructuring and resume distributions to unitholders. The agreement is subject to unitholders’ passing resolutions at a Dec 15 extraordinary general meeting. Under the agreement, lenders would waive certain conditions under the Reit’s 2023 master restructuring agreement, and extend loans by about 12 to 18 months, excluding the sponsor-lender loan. Units of the trust ended flat at US$0.031 before the announcement.

Trading halt: Keppel and Starhub called for a trading halt on Tuesday morning, pending the release of an announcement. StarHub then announced that it has agreed to merge with Keppel’s M1 in an all-share deal. It also exercised an option to buy Circles Life’s Singapore mobile business. Shares of Keppel closed S$0.02 or 0.2 per cent lower at S$8.83 on Monday, while shares of StarHub closed S$0.01 or 1 per cent lower at S$1.01.

data.title: Morgan Stanley trims tech exposure amid tensions, flags S’pore, other Asian defensive winners
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The global artificial intelligence build-out recently has had some headwinds, including the US midterm election results as well as US chip curbs announced last week.

The new US rule restricts shipments of advanced chips to South-east Asian countries such as Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models.

Morgan Stanley says that Asean capacity forecasts for data centres and powers are lowered as a result, and that it is a negative for China-linked cloud operators. 

“The key bottleneck we see in China remains the ability to produce manufacture compute. That creates greater uncertainty around access to compute and will only reinforce the push for self-sufficiency. For Southeast Asia, I think it will depend on how the industry works through the finer details,” Daniel Blake, Asia equity and thematic strategist, told reporters at a briefing this week. Compute is a term for process power and hardware resources.

But Jonathan Garner, chief Asia and emerging market strategist, sounded an optimistic note at the same briefing.

“Just data-centred capex in Asia generally is not very large within the overall investment theme. Other areas like industrial and energy are much much bigger. So it won’t affect the economic growth outlook very much for the countries in Southeast Asia.”

In the wake of the US midterms, where several Democrat candidates won on the opposition to the data centre build-out, these projects in the US are expected to slow temporarily. That has raised fears on the impact on China’s AI-driven growth as well, said a Bloomberg report.

Winners – or the more defensive – and losers

There are areas of the market that are more defensive amid these geopolitical risks, however.

Morgan Stanley reiterated its overweight positions on Japan and South Korea.

“Japan and (South) Korea... are less impacted by the more restrictive trade and export controls environment… Both offer diversified thematic exposure, including key links into the capex super-cycle, which derives more from industrial, defence and energy investment than AI end-markets,” said Morgan Stanley in a report, by analysts led by Garner.

On the other hand, it is broadly more negative for Taiwan due to heightened US-China tensions, it said.

As for Chinese markets, the bank has a preference for onshore shares, versus offshore and MSCI China shares.

The more restrictive trade environment will affect, to some extent, the business models of key large-cap listed – as well as unlisted – companies that benefited from the use of third-country data centres as part of their AI development strategy, said Morgan Stanley.

The risk premium for foreign investors – in offshore China equities – is also likely raised, amid ongoing US-China trade tensions and tech restrictions, among other factors, it said.

“In contrast, there is a potential benefit for the rapidly growing AI supply chain localisation beneficiaries, mainly listed in the A-share market,” the bank added.

Overall, in terms of less volatile parts of the market, there has been a pivot towards AI adopters as beneficiaries, said Garner, where previously much of the focus was on AI upstream such as semiconductors.

He added that the bank has recently been shifting its recommended focus list stocks towards consumer staples and firms with high free cash flow that can offer “more defensive exposure,” while reducing its overweight position in tech and industrials.

The bank said, however, there is an “increment negative from an investor risk perception” for Singapore, Brazil, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia – although it is unlikely to affect the growth outlook.

“The US authorities have specifically identified these countries as representing risk in relation to illegal transhipment of advance chips to China. It is important however to observe that the roll-out of data centres serving US multinationals and hyperscalers is not impacted,” said Morgan Stanley.

But Blake pointed out one theme that is keeping some of these countries afloat in times of heightened risks.

“In parallel, we’re seeing improvements in corporate governance across Japan, South Korea and Singapore, as well as efforts in Thailand and Malaysia to improve governance quality and returns,” he said, naming industrials, defence stocks and companies exposed to sovereign AI.

“Alongside the global AI investment narrative, there is also a corporate reform and reinvestment story that may be underappreciated,” said Blake. “There will certainly be winners and losers, with some markets better positioned than others.”

Singapore is top defensive market

Garner said that amid potential geopolitical and supply chain risks, Singapore stands out as the most defensive market in Asia-Pacific.

“We’ve been structurally very bullish on Singapore, and it has outperformed over the cycle. ROE has improved meaningfully in recent years. Singapore is a AAA-rated sovereign with a large current account surplus and would be highly resilient relative to other countries in an adverse global scenario in 2027, should that materialize,” said Garner.

data.title: Shein’s slow India restart lays bare limits of billionaire Ambani’s retail might
data.description:
SHEIN Global Holdings’ return to India through a local partner is off to a slow start, due to supply chain snags, leadership uncertainty and a lack of proprietary technology that made the fast-fashion brand a hit. 

It relaunched in February 2025, hoping to ride the retail might of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, but the venture has struggled to regain its former glory, people familiar with the matter said, speaking on condition of anonymity about private matters.

User adoption remains weak: the app averaged about 6 million monthly active users in October, down from the previous month and broadly unchanged from January levels, according to estimates shared by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

By comparison, market leader Myntra, an indirect unit of Walmart, averaged about 100 million monthly active users.

These metrics are a far cry from Shein’s 2017 debut in the country, when it drew hordes of customers looking for trendy clothes and pocket-friendly prices.

It was then among dozens of Chinese apps, including TikTok, that New Delhi banned in 2020 over security concerns. Before the ban, India accounted for 67 per cent of Shein’s monthly active users in 2019, according to Sensor Tower.

The tepid restart is a challenge for Isha Ambani, the Ambani scion who oversees the conglomerate’s consumer business.

Reliance Retail’s stable includes partnerships with a gamut of global brands like Marks & Spencer, Pret A Manger, Hamleys and Sephora, a broad range that risks causing the enterprise to sag under its own weight.

For Shein, the underwhelming India partnership means it cannot lean on the world’s most populous nation for growth as it battles weak demand in Europe and the US, its two biggest markets.

Reliance is in charge of all operations in India, including product selection, marketing and sales, the people said.

As a result, Shein has not shared its proprietary technology that allows the Chinese giant to to spot, design and produce new styles in less than 10 days. Reliance has thus had to build critical processes — from vendor onboarding to production workflows — from scratch, the people said. 

Reliance also lacks Shein’s vast manufacturing network in China. It has tapped smaller Indian makers to produce the apparel instead, many of which are not accustomed to producing the Gen-Z focused styles the brand is known for.

Suppliers have had to adjust to unusually specific requirements, resulting in additional training, higher wastage, and longer turnaround times, people familiar said. 

Employees have also had to compete internally for funds and management attention, given Reliance Retail’s sprawling collection of businesses and rapidly expanding brand portfolio.

Early leadership churn added to the uncertainty. Former Meta Platforms executive Manish Chopra, who was helping Reliance set up the Shein venture, left the group in 2024 within a year of joining, according to his LinkedIn profile.

Shein and Reliance Retail did not respond to queries from Bloomberg News. Chopra declined to comment.

The broader market has also shifted.

India’s online fashion and lifestyle segment — projected to reach US$45 billion by 2028 — has become crowded during Shein’s absence. Myntra, Tata Group’s Trent, Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail and upstarts like Meesho have broadened their appeal among India’s price-sensitive consumers.

“Shein is reentering a market that is already incredibly competitive,” Kara Lee, senior insights analyst at Sensor Tower said. “There’s just a stronger natural consumer preference toward brands that have been able to exist in that space this entire time.”

Consumer engagement reflects that pivot. Shein users in India spent about four minutes a week on the app over the past two months, below the global average of 6.6 minutes, according to Sensor Tower estimates. 

Download trends paint an even bleaker picture: despite a 60 per cent year-on-year increase in advertising spending in September, downloads fell 73 per cent from a year earlier to 790,000. They declined further to 740,000 in the following month. 

Even when Shein was among India’s largest advertisers in May, the app barely entered the top 40 on the Apple app store, suggesting diminishing returns on marketing, according to Sensor Tower’s Lee. It was an unranked app in early November.

NextGen Fast Fashion, the Reliance unit operating Shein India, recorded 4.4 million rupees (US$48,136) in revenue for the year ended Mar 31, compared with Reliance Retail’s nearly 3.7 trillion rupees overall.

Stark difference

For shoppers like Sophin Chhettri, a 25-year-old fashion professional in New Delhi, the difference in Shein’s second act in India is stark. 

She once turned to Shein for inexpensive jewellery and trinkets with “hip and new designs that you would typically see in the West and on the internet but wasn’t easily accessible in India,” she said. “I’ve not even seen the new site,” she said.

To be sure, Reliance can leverage the strength of its wide-ranging fashion offerings — which includes e-retailer Ajio and apparel store brands such as Reliance Trends — to boost Shein India’s success.

Reliance can benefit if it can bundle all its retail apparel offerings into one umbrella, according to Karan Taurani, analyst at Elara Securities Pvt. “That is one good strategy.”

Globally, Shein has pivoted to markets such as Brazil, the US, and Mexico since the 2020 India ban. India now accounts for just 2 per cent of its audience, according to Sensor Tower data.

Its profit from this market came in at 3.9 million rupees (US$42,282) in the year ended March 2026, compared to global profit of US$2.1 billion in 2025.

Still, Reliance is not giving up. A broader marketing campaign is expected early next year, people familiar said. 

“Reliance has always been about dominance through scale and rapid growth,” said Devangshu Dutta, founder of consultancy Third Eyesight. “I don’t think that Shein in its second coming with Reliance has been able to build that yet.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: European leaders dig in on budget disputes as talks stall
data.description:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said European Union leaders called off a second day of budget talks in Brussels on Friday (Nov 27), as countries refused to budge in negotiations over the bloc’s long-term funding plan.

THE leaders had gathered on Thursday morning for a summit meant to create momentum for a December deal over the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which runs from 2028 to 2034. 

Within hours, however, officials were privately grumbling about how the negotiations were evolving as countries stuck to their long-entrenched positions, according to people familiar with the matter. They requested anonymity in order to speak freely about the meeting.

Several participants focused their ire on European Council President Antonio Costa, who oversees EU summits, with some questioning the strategy behind the meeting. In the end, leaders conceded they were simply too far apart.

“There are far too many efforts that need to be taken,” Merz told reporters late on Thursday. “Far too much work that needs to be done.”

The tensions risk imperiling a year-end deadline the EU has set to finalise its near-2 trillion-euro (US$2.2 trillion) budget, a vital source of funding for Europe’s farmers, infrastructure projects and defence. 

The timing is meant to prevent the talks from being swept into France’s election, where far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading in the polls and has been calling for cuts to EU budget contributions.

“We’re light years away” from a budget solution, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told reporters on the summit’s sidelines.

In truth, the plan on Thursday was never to reach a deal — at least not yet — but to suss out where there might be room to manoeuvre. Costa first asked all 27 EU leaders to meet together, before sending them into a series of smaller groups for 30-minute chats to test for potential compromises.

Leaders were set to then reconvene around midnight to determine whether it was worth staying until Friday to keep talking. 

But before that meeting even happened, some of them decided against it.

It was evident, the people said, that countries remained far apart on critical issues, ranging from the budget’s overall size to new EU taxes to how much money should be spent on narrowing economic gaps between regions.

Some officials left angry, arguing there had been little reason to hold the discussion while leaders remained so divided. Ambassadors, they noted, can discuss procedural matters.

A person close to Costa pushed back on the notion, insisting the discussions concerned fundamental political issues that needed leaders’ input.

The person stressed that even if everyone was repeating well-known stances, the breakout sessions offered a chance to advance the discussions and identify areas of convergence.

The EU’s budget divides tend to be a mixture of regional, economic or ideological disagreements.

Broadly speaking, wealthier EU countries across the west and north — which contribute more than they receive from the bloc’s budget — want a smaller budget.

“We cannot be an ATM for the European Union,” said Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. 

Countries across the south and further east, however, have been defending a larger EU budget that retains significant funds to lift up less-affluent regions.

“Cohesion is really the goal of the European Union and the Czech Republic,” said Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis. “We will fight for this money.”

At the core of the fights are shifting beliefs about what values should infuse the EU budget. 

Historically, a large chunk of the bloc’s money has gone toward agriculture, for instance, supporting farmers’ income and food production.

While countries still consider that essential, there have been calls to also spend more on helping companies grow and compete with the US and China — a change linked to anxiety that Europe must spur economic activity and cut reliance on foreign partners.

Additionally, numerous leaders say the EU budget must prioritise defence spending — something it historically eschewed. With Moscow menacing and the US pulling back from the continent, many countries, especially those closer to the Russian border, say it’s now a vital part of the EU’s mission.

“A cheap Europe could turn out to be a very expensive mistake,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in a social media post during the meeting. “Security comes at a price. As simple as that.”

By this logic, funding for Ukraine has been pulled into the EU budget talks. 

EU leaders are trying to finalize a new 45 billion-euro (US$49.2 billion) loan for Kyiv as the country’s financial needs escalate nearly five years into Russia’s full-scale war.

While that money would be separate from the EU budget, economic heavyweights like Germany and the Netherlands are saying that if countries don’t participate in the loan, they shouldn’t enjoy certain EU budget benefits.

Those seeking an opt-out from the loan, including Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, did not back down on Thursday, insisting the two issues shouldn’t be linked.

But the topic didn’t feature much into the conversation once leaders got in the room, the people said, and the loan itself isn’t at risk.

For now, talks will continue at lower levels, with the hopes that compromises can be found between now and a summit planned for Dec 17 and 18, a Thursday and Friday. Already, officials are signaling that the gathering may go straight through the weekend.

“We all want to be home by Christmas,” Merz said. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Human oversight in AI should be measured, not assumed
data.description:
RECENT reports in The Business Times have highlighted that clear permissions, audit trails, well-governed data and human sign-off on consequential decisions are key safeguards for financial institutions deploying artificial intelligence agents.

But keeping a human in the loop is not, by itself, a sufficient control. The more useful question is what risk that human checkpoint is meant to reduce, and whether it actually does so.

At the recent Global Finance & Technology Network session on AI innovation and governance, I asked a senior leader at a global bank whether an agent’s mandate could change in real time as conditions changed. The response was candid. It was a difficult question requiring further analysis.

That matters because human review can become a significant constraint as agentic workflows scale. McKinsey found that for a banking customer-service agent, human oversight accounted for 70 to 75 per cent of variable run costs, compared with 20 to 25 per cent for token costs.

The figures will differ across workflows, but they expose an important trade-off. Applying human approval too broadly can undermine the efficiency automation is meant to create.

Oversight should therefore follow the risk. A suspected fraud case, rejected loan, or large transfer to a new counterparty may warrant human judgment.

An agent assembling documents or updating an internal workflow within tightly defined permissions may not. The relevant factors include customer impact, value at risk, reversibility and uncertainty.

That principle is consistent with the AI risk-management guidelines from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), which urge financial institutions to apply controls proportionately according to their risk exposure and the scale and nature of their AI use.

MAS’ Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime Framework complements that direction with more granular guidance on how agent actions can be authorised, recorded and escalated for human review.

Banks should apply the same discipline to human oversight.

There is no single formula for assessing whether a checkpoint works. The industry will need evidence on where intervention catches material problems, changes proposed actions or adds delay without reducing risk.

A checkpoint may remain necessary for audit or accountability, even if interventions are rare.

The bank should be able to explain what risk it controls.

Crucially, this rule book cannot remain static. Agents act at machine speed, while the policies, mandates and controls governing them still change at human speed.

As agents take on new tasks, banks will need to revisit whether their escalation points still match the risks.

The goal is not maximum autonomy or maximum human involvement; it is to put human judgment where it changes the outcome. Every escalation should have a clear purpose.

Wei You Pan Field chief technology officer, MongoDB
